- adr: Apply when an architectural decision was just made — one shaping system structure, boundaries, or a contract other code depends on — or when asked to write or review an Architecture Decision Record.
- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository.
- rust-style: Apply when writing or modifying Rust code in this project.
- rust-types: Apply when defining new public structs or enums.
- rustdoc: Apply when writing doc comments on public Rust items.
- courier:changeset: Trigger when the user asks to add a changeset or document a change: "add a changeset", "document this change", "what changed here". Extracts the consumer-facing meaning of a diff: classifies consumer_impact (behavior-change, new-capability, internal-only) and semver_impact (major, minor, patch, none) per shared/references/delivery/changesets.md's decision table, then writes a summary scaled to that classification. A diff spanning multiple independent topics — common on a backlog/catch-up run, not just a single PR — produces one changeset per topic, not one bundled entry. When the change came via smith, pass along implementer's criteria_evidence — changeset-analyzer uses those exact locations instead of reconstructing approximate ones from the diff.
- courier:commit: Trigger when the user asks to commit code or write a commit message: "commit this", "write a commit message", "commit the staged changes". Reads the staged git diff and produces a conventional commit message explaining why the change was made, not what changed — the diff already shows what changed.
- courier:post-review: Trigger when the user has an already-drafted review or reply and wants it posted: "post this review", "reply to this comment", "mark this thread resolved", "submit my review comments". Takes drafted content — from the built-in `code-review` skill's findings, from `courier/receive-feedback`'s response plan, or typed directly by the user — and posts it to GitHub via `gh pr review` or `gh pr comment`. Does not draft content itself; this skill is purely mechanical execution of something already written, gated by explicit user confirmation before any post fires.
- courier:pr: Trigger when the user asks to open a PR or write a PR description: "open a PR", "create a pull request", "write the PR description". Given a diff, a linked spec, and a linked requirement, produces a PR title and body a reviewer with zero context can act on, then opens the PR via `gh pr create` after user confirmation.
- courier:receive-feedback: Trigger when the user asks to process or triage incoming review feedback: "address the feedback", "respond to review comments", "what do these comments mean", "triage this review". Assembles a review package — diff summary, linked spec, test results, open questions — so the author has full context to respond without re-reading the whole thread. Does not categorize individual comments by priority; that's the caller's judgment call, made with `shared/references/delivery/github.md`'s vocabulary in hand. This is for feedback received on the user's own PR — critiquing someone else's PR is the built-in `code-review` skill's job, not this one.
- courier:release: Trigger when the user asks to cut a release or summarize what's in one: "cut a release", "what's in this release", "generate release notes". Aggregates changeset@2 entries since the last release into a release-artifact@2: filters consumer_impact: internal-only entries, computes the version as max(semver_impact) across the rest applied to the prior version, and carries each changeset's summary through unedited.
- muse:component: Trigger when the user asks to spec a UI component: "spec this component", "draft a component spec", "write a spec for this design", "audit this component spec", "is this component spec ready?", "gate this component spec". Given a requirement@1 or free-text design intent, produces a spec@1 covering props, variants, per-state observable behavior, and accessibility criteria as testable propositions. Every criterion is falsifiable from outside the implementation; error cases and invalid prop combinations carry is_error_case: true. No TBDs anywhere in the document — genuinely unknown items go in non_goals or the reasoning scratchpad instead. Gated by a binding exit gate before the spec proceeds to planning.
- navigator:plan: Trigger this skill when the user says "write a plan for X", "how do we implement this spec", "break this down into tasks", "what are the implementation steps", "create an implementation plan", or "plan this out". Produces a plan@1 artifact where every task includes exact file paths, a brief implementation approach, exact implementation code, the exact tests proving each criterion, a conventional commit message, and covers_criteria linking the task to specific acceptance criteria. spec_file_path and linked_requirement are propagated from the source spec. No TBDs. No "implement as appropriate." Every step is mechanically executable by a developer with zero domain context.
- ranger:audit: Find evidence-backed reachable defects in Rust, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, or Go. Refute candidates, group defect families, and verify fixes against current code and the relevant execution boundary.
- scribe:architect: Trigger when `finding-report@2`, `implementation-review@2`, or `implementation-result@1` identifies a structural defect class. Produce the smallest `spec@1` that makes recurrence impossible or machine-detectable through a type, API, boundary, invariant, lint, test, or CI rule.
- scribe:audit-architecture: Trigger when a draft spec@1 needs checking against the workspace's whole-system architecture — not another spec, and not a single signature — before it reaches scribe/gate-spec: "check this spec against our architecture", "does this fit the system", "audit this against the arch model". Given a spec@1, checks it against the persisted arch-model@2 for boundary violations, competing abstractions, and invariant conflicts, building or refreshing the model first if it's absent or stale for the area the spec touches. Returns specific, rewritten fixes on fail, the same standard as scribe/audit-spec but at system scope instead of spec scope.
- scribe:audit-spec: Trigger when the user asks to review a spec's quality: "review this spec", "is this spec complete?", "audit this spec". Given a spec@1, adversarially reviews it for untestable criteria, ambiguous language, missing error cases, scope overlap with other specs, and incomplete sections. Returns a structured issue list with specific rewritten suggested fixes, not generic guidance. Named audit-spec rather than audit because the bare word audit is already ranger's plugin-level skill name (code/bug auditing) — a different domain entirely.
- scribe:correct-spec: Trigger when implementer reports that a spec criterion contradicts what the system actually does: a spec_contradiction status from smith. Given a spec_file_path, the criterion_id of the affected acceptance criterion, and a contradiction report (what the spec says vs. what the system actually does), revises the affected criterion — and any criteria that depend on it — and returns a corrected spec@1 with revision_note set. Use this when implementation reveals the spec itself is wrong, not merely hard to satisfy.
- scribe:draft-spec: Trigger when the user asks to write or draft a spec: "spec this out", "draft a spec", "write a spec for this requirement". Given a requirement@1 and optionally a research-report@1, produces a spec@1 draft with purpose, scope, non_goals, api_surface (if applicable), and acceptance criteria. Every criterion is a testable proposition; error cases carry is_error_case: true. No TBDs anywhere in the document — genuinely unknown items go in non_goals or the reasoning scratchpad instead.
- scribe:gate-spec: Trigger when a spec@1 needs a definitive pass/fail judgment before it enters planning: "gate this spec", "is this spec ready?", "check this spec before we plan it". Default disposition is fail — the spec must earn a pass. Passes only if every acceptance criterion is testable with no vague language, no TBDs remain, error cases are explicitly covered, and scope is narrow enough for one planning cycle. On fail, returns blockers specific enough for scribe/draft-spec to act on without further clarification.
- scribe:spec-drift: Trigger when the user asks whether implemented code still matches its spec, weeks or months after implementation: "check spec drift", "does the code still match this spec?", "has this spec drifted?". Given a spec@1 (via spec_file_path) and a workspace root, reads the spec from disk and the implementation from the workspace, and reports each criterion as covered (implemented and tested), uncovered (no matching implementation), or drifted (implementation exists but diverges from the criterion's contract). Every criterion is a testable proposition; error cases carry is_error_case: true. No TBDs anywhere in the document — genuinely unknown items go in non_goals or the reasoning scratchpad instead.
- scribe:gate-spec: Trigger when a spec@1 needs a definitive pass/fail judgment before it enters planning: "gate this spec", "is this spec ready?", "check this spec before we plan it". Default disposition is fail — the spec must earn a pass. Passes only if every acceptance criterion is testable with no vague language, no TBDs remain, error cases are explicitly covered, and scope is narrow enough for one planning cycle. This gate checks the spec on its own terms — whole-system architectural fit is scribe/audit-architecture's job upstream, not re-litigated here. On fail, returns blockers specific enough for scribe/draft-spec to act on without further clarification.
- scribe:spec-drift: Trigger when the user asks whether implemented code still matches its spec, weeks or months after implementation: "check spec drift", "does the code still match this spec?", "has this spec drifted?". Given a spec@1 (via spec_file_path) and a workspace root, reads the spec from disk and the implementation from the workspace, and reports each criterion as covered (implemented and tested), uncovered (no matching implementation), or drifted (implementation exists but diverges from the criterion's contract). This is an on-demand diagnostic, not a blocking gate — scribe/gate-spec is the blocking gate.
- scribe:verify-spec: Trigger when the user asks whether a spec matches its source: "is this grounded?", "does this spec match the requirement?", "check this spec against the requirement". Given a draft spec@1 plus the originating requirement@1 and optional research-report@1, checks whether each acceptance criterion is grounded in the source artifacts. Classifies criteria as supported, unsupported, or overfitted. Collects evidence only — does not produce a pass/fail verdict. Use before implementation, not after — for post-implementation drift, use scribe/spec-drift instead.
- sentinel:gate: Trigger this skill when the user says "verify this", "check this spec", "check this plan", "check this requirement", "check this PR", "is this done?", "review this for completeness", "does this meet the criteria?", "gate this", or "quality check" — also before stage transitions: starting implementation from a spec, shipping from an implementation, opening a PR from a branch. Applies to any stage artifact: requirements, specs, plans, implementations, PRs. Do not activate for general Q&A, code explanation, or exploratory work with no artifact boundary being crossed. The gate either clears the artifact for the next stage or returns specific, actionable blockers to the producing agent.
- smith:implement: Activate for implementation, implementation tests, or behavior-preserving refactoring. Execute bounded batches with risk-based verification, defect-family review, and an independent scoped verdict. Do not activate for explanation-only requests.
- vanguard:research: Activate when the user says "I need to understand X before deciding", "is there a way to do Y", "what are the options for Z", "research this", "investigate this", "what does the codebase already do for X", "prior art on Y", or "what are the risks of approach Z" — also when the approach for a spec or plan is unclear, when checking what dependencies exist for a feature, or when any design question needs an evidence base before commitment. Investigates the question across internal sources (specs, docs, codebase patterns, manifests) and external sources as needed, then produces a research-report@1 that distinguishes confirmed findings from likely inferences from unverified assumptions, with a falsifiable recommendation and explicit confidence level so a spec writer (scribe) isn't surprised by implementation reality.
- weaver:audit-backlog: Trigger when the user asks about overall backlog health: "what's in the backlog", "audit the backlog", "what requirements are missing coverage". Cross-references all open requirement@1 objects against existing specs and implementation files. Returns per-requirement status (covered, partial, missing, duplicate) with evidence, plus a structured summary — per-status counts and an optional one-clause note, not a prose paragraph. Named audit-backlog rather than bare audit because that word is already ranger's plugin-level skill name (code/bug auditing) — a different domain entirely.
- weaver:capture-need: Trigger when the user describes a raw need in free text: "we need X", "the problem is Y", "users are asking for Z". Converts unstructured text into a structured requirement@1 draft — id, statement, stakeholder, why, done_when — without asking clarifying questions. Fields that cannot be inferred are omitted, not fabricated. out_of_scope is intentionally left empty for weaver/connect-requirement or a human to fill in.
- weaver:clarify-requirement: Trigger when a requirement@1 draft from weaver/capture-need has gaps to close before a spec can be written: "is this requirement complete?", "what's missing from this requirement". Given a requirement@1, evaluates gaps in priority order — testability of done_when, specificity of stakeholder, explicitness of out_of_scope — and either asks one focused question or returns the completed requirement with out_of_scope populated. One question per invocation, never a list.
- weaver:connect-requirement: Trigger when the user asks whether a specific requirement already exists or relates to other work: "is this already captured?", "does this overlap with an existing requirement?", "what does this relate to?". Given one requirement@1 (or a small named set), searches the workspace for related specs and implementation files, and checks for duplicate or overlapping requirements. Returns coverage status and duplicate_of references scoped to just the requirement(s) given — not a full backlog sweep.
- weaver:prioritize-backlog: Trigger when the user asks what to work on first from a set of requirements: "what should we prioritize", "rank the backlog", "what's most urgent". Given a list of requirement@1 drafts, ranks them by impact, urgency, and dependency order — a requirement another depends on ranks above the one depending on it, even if its own impact/urgency score is lower. Returns an ordered list with a concrete rationale per requirement.
- mason:audit-plugin: Audit an existing plugin against repository authoring, schema, wiring, and packaging rules. Use for plugin conformance or release-readiness checks. Return an evidence-backed pass, fail, or warning for each check without modifying files.
- mason:design-schema: Trigger when the user wants to design a new inter-agent artifact schema: "design a schema for X", "add a new schema to shared/schemas", "what should this handoff look like?". Given a description of what the artifact represents, who produces it, and who consumes it, produces a JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) following ecosystem conventions — $id as name@version, additionalProperties false, a reasoning scratchpad field, all fields documented — and checks for conflicts with existing schemas.
- mason:evaluate: Evaluate a plugin workflow against a fixed behavioral fixture. Use for release gates, Claude/Codex comparisons, regression checks, and longitudinal plugin quality analysis. Preserve exact execution provenance and hidden-oracle isolation.
- mason:scaffold-plugin: Create a complete plugin from an ID and purpose. Use for new plugin requests. Generate the manifest, skill, cognitive-mode agents, shared linkage, routing, and any required schema contracts; validate the result before handoff.
- mason:scaffold-subagent: Add one conformant agent to an existing plugin. Use when the request names an agent task and tier without requesting a new plugin. Create only the agent file and report required routing; leave unrelated plugin files unchanged.
- cowork-plugin-management:cowork-plugin-customizer: Customize a Claude Code plugin for a specific organization's tools and workflows. # RTK - Rust Token Killer

**Usage**: Token-optimized CLI proxy (60-90% savings on dev operations)

## Meta Commands (always use rtk directly)

```bash
rtk gain              # Show token savings analytics
rtk gain --history    # Show command usage history with savings
rtk discover          # Analyze Claude Code history for missed opportunities
rtk proxy <cmd>       # Execute raw command without filtering (for debugging)
```

## Installation Verification

```bash
rtk --version         # Should show: rtk X.Y.Z
rtk gain              # Should work (not "command not found")
which rtk             # Verify correct binary
```

⚠️ **Name collision**: If `rtk gain` fails, you may have reachingforthejack/rtk (Rust Type Kit) installed instead.

## Hook-Based Usage

All other commands are automatically rewritten by the Claude Code hook.
Example: `git status` → `rtk git status` (transparent, 0 tokens overhead)

Refer to CLAUDE.md for full command reference.

# CLAUDE.md

@AGENTS.md

This file adds only what's specific to Claude Code.

## Skills

- **`superpowers:test-driven-development`** before writing implementation code for any command or module. The spec's fixtures (`tests/fixtures/small-ts/`) exist to drive this.
- **`superpowers:systematic-debugging`** before proposing a fix for a test failure or unexpected behavior.
- **`superpowers:brainstorming`** before any design change not already covered by `docs/adr/` or `docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md`.

## Verification

Before claiming a command or module works, run it against the fixtures in `docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md`'s "Test fixtures" section, not just `cargo check`.

# monokl

AST-aware code search for TypeScript, JavaScript and Rust, built for coding agents. Part of [Orin DX](https://orin-dx.com) (github.com/orin-dx). Agent-facing output goes through [michi](https://github.com/orin-dx/michi) (`michi-core` on crates.io); don't hand-roll TOON lists, structured errors or hints that michi provides.

Vendor-neutral guidance. [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) adds Claude Code specifics.

## Read first

1. [`docs/spec/README.md`](docs/spec/README.md): which spec file covers what. The spec is the reconstruction source for unbuilt modules.
2. [`docs/architecture/README.md`](docs/architecture/README.md): which topic doc to read for the area you're changing.
3. [`docs/adr/README.md`](docs/adr/README.md) and [`docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md`](docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md): decisions already made. If something looks inconsistent, check here before "fixing" it.
4. [PRINCIPLES.md](PRINCIPLES.md): non-goals. No embedding reranker, no persistent trigram index, no tree-sitter TS/JS parser.

## Commands

```bash
just setup      # proto toolchain + moon git hooks
just ci         # everything CI runs
just test       # nextest + doctests
just lint       # fmt check + clippy, all features and no default features
```

Run one cargo command at a time; parallel cargo processes serialize on the `target/` lock. Never `git checkout Cargo.lock`.

## Current state

One crate, `crates/monokl`, with the error types, core data types, query language, text search, ranking, the TypeScript analyzer (parse and extract), the search pipeline and `monokl search`. Modules are declared in `lib.rs` as they are implemented, not ahead of time, and a dependency is listed only once code uses it. [`.claude/plans/ACTIVE.md`](.claude/plans/ACTIVE.md) tracks what's next.

## Non-negotiables

- No `unwrap()`/`expect()`/`panic!()`/`unreachable!()`/`unimplemented!()` outside `#[cfg(test)]`. The workspace lint table denies them.
- One `thiserror` error enum, `MonoklError`. Compose failure modes with `#[from]`/`#[source]`; no `String`-message variant when a structured one is possible. File I/O failures are `FileIoError` ([ADR 0001](docs/adr/0001-file-io-error-lives-in-monokl.md)).
- `LanguageAnalyzer` implementations return fully owned data. No arena-borrowed AST node or parser-allocator lifetime in any field of `FileAnalysis`.
- `camino::Utf8Path`/`Utf8PathBuf` wherever a path appears.
- `FxHashMap`/`FxHashSet` for internal hot-path maps; `BTreeMap` for anything serialized, because output order must be deterministic.
- Core result types are not `Serialize`; wire shapes live in the output layer. See [`08-library-session-api.md`](docs/spec/08-library-session-api.md#9-plumbing-and-porcelain-two-crates).
- No caps or pre-rendered truncation strings in core. Counts only (`items_returned`/`items_total`); the output layer renders the marker.
- `unsafe_code` is denied workspace-wide.

## Rust style

Skills in [`.agents/skills/`](.agents/skills/) hold the detail: `rust-style` (control flow, matching, naming), `rust-types` (public type checklist, "wire or don't define"), `rustdoc` (doc comment format), `adr`.

- `pub(crate)` for implementation modules; `pub` only for the consumer API.
- No wildcard `_` arm on enums this crate owns; a compile error on a new variant is the point.
- Code never cites spec, criterion or plan IDs (`SPEC-001`, `AC-007`, `T-009`). Specs change; the code says what it guarantees in its own words, and tests name the behavior they prove.

## Testing

- `cargo nextest` plus `cargo test --doc`. `insta` for snapshots: accept a snapshot change only after confirming the new output is correct, not just different.
- Assert content, not presence: `assert_eq!` on the exact value over `contains`/`is_some`.
- Sibling-path parity: a function that mirrors an already-tested one gets a test asserting the same contract.
- CI gates line coverage at 90%.

## Fixing bugs

Look for structurally identical siblings and fix them in the same change. If one is deliberately left, say where and why.

When the spec itself is wrong, fix the spec file and add an entry to [`05-research-and-decisions.md`](docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md) explaining what was wrong and why the fix is right. A decision that departs from the spec with a credible alternative gets an ADR.

## Writing and commits

- Succinct: short sentences, bullets, tables. No backstory, hedging or filler. Banned words are in [`docs/adr/README.md`](docs/adr/README.md).
- Never hard-wrap Markdown, commit messages or PR descriptions.
- Comments explain only the non-obvious why, carry no history (the commit records it), and fill to 120 columns.
- Commits: Conventional Commits, imperative subject, at most one or two sentences of why. Skip the body when the subject says it all.

- [Working style](working-style-light-process.md) — light ceremony, parallel worktrees, stacked draft PRs, user merges, never force-push
- [Orin DX suite](orin-dx-suite.md) — org is orin-dx (no more orin-axi); callisto/caliper are the convention references; michi for output
- [Monokl spec overview](monokl-spec-overview.md) — index of docs/monokl-spec.md's 4 parts so it needn't be fully re-read
- [OXC analyzer patterns](oxc-analyzer-patterns.md) — arena containment, visitor pattern, gotchas from oxc-react-docgen
- [Monokl vs codegraph](monokl-vs-codegraph.md) — competitive analysis recommendations, not yet adopted

# monokl

AST-aware code search for TypeScript, JavaScript and Rust, built for coding agents. Part of [Orin DX](https://orin-dx.com) (github.com/orin-dx). Agent-facing output goes through [michi](https://github.com/orin-dx/michi) (`michi-core` on crates.io); don't hand-roll TOON lists, structured errors or hints that michi provides.

Vendor-neutral guidance. [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) adds Claude Code specifics.

## Read first

1. [`docs/spec/README.md`](docs/spec/README.md): which spec file covers what. The spec is the reconstruction source for unbuilt modules.
2. [`docs/architecture/README.md`](docs/architecture/README.md): which topic doc to read for the area you're changing.
3. [`docs/adr/README.md`](docs/adr/README.md) and [`docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md`](docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md): decisions already made. If something looks inconsistent, check here before "fixing" it.
4. [PRINCIPLES.md](PRINCIPLES.md): non-goals. No embedding reranker, no persistent trigram index, no tree-sitter TS/JS parser.

## Commands

```bash
just setup      # proto toolchain + moon git hooks
just ci         # everything CI runs
just test       # nextest + doctests
just lint       # fmt check + clippy, all features and no default features
```

Run one cargo command at a time; parallel cargo processes serialize on the `target/` lock. Never `git checkout Cargo.lock`.

## Current state

One crate, `crates/monokl`, with the error types, core data types, query language, text search, ranking, the TypeScript analyzer (parse and extract), the search pipeline and `monokl search`. Modules are declared in `lib.rs` as they are implemented, not ahead of time, and a dependency is listed only once code uses it. [`.claude/plans/ACTIVE.md`](.claude/plans/ACTIVE.md) tracks what's next.

## Non-negotiables

- No `unwrap()`/`expect()`/`panic!()`/`unreachable!()`/`unimplemented!()` outside `#[cfg(test)]`. The workspace lint table denies them.
- One `thiserror` error enum, `MonoklError`. Compose failure modes with `#[from]`/`#[source]`; no `String`-message variant when a structured one is possible. File I/O failures are `FileIoError` ([ADR 0001](docs/adr/0001-file-io-error-lives-in-monokl.md)).
- `LanguageAnalyzer` implementations return fully owned data. No arena-borrowed AST node or parser-allocator lifetime in any field of `FileAnalysis`.
- `camino::Utf8Path`/`Utf8PathBuf` wherever a path appears.
- `FxHashMap`/`FxHashSet` for internal hot-path maps; `BTreeMap` for anything serialized, because output order must be deterministic.
- Core result types are not `Serialize`; wire shapes live in the output layer. See [`08-library-session-api.md`](docs/spec/08-library-session-api.md#9-plumbing-and-porcelain-two-crates).
- No caps or pre-rendered truncation strings in core. Counts only (`items_returned`/`items_total`); the output layer renders the marker.
- `unsafe_code` is denied workspace-wide.

## Rust style

Skills in [`.agents/skills/`](.agents/skills/) hold the detail: `rust-style` (control flow, matching, naming), `rust-types` (public type checklist, "wire or don't define"), `rustdoc` (doc comment format), `adr`.

- `pub(crate)` for implementation modules; `pub` only for the consumer API.
- No wildcard `_` arm on enums this crate owns; a compile error on a new variant is the point.
- Code never cites spec, criterion or plan IDs (`SPEC-001`, `AC-007`, `T-009`). Specs change; the code says what it guarantees in its own words, and tests name the behavior they prove.

## Testing

- `cargo nextest` plus `cargo test --doc`. `insta` for snapshots: accept a snapshot change only after confirming the new output is correct, not just different.
- Assert content, not presence: `assert_eq!` on the exact value over `contains`/`is_some`.
- Sibling-path parity: a function that mirrors an already-tested one gets a test asserting the same contract.
- CI gates line coverage at 90%.

## Fixing bugs

Look for structurally identical siblings and fix them in the same change. If one is deliberately left, say where and why.

When the spec itself is wrong, fix the spec file and add an entry to [`05-research-and-decisions.md`](docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md) explaining what was wrong and why the fix is right. A decision that departs from the spec with a credible alternative gets an ADR.

## Writing and commits

- Succinct: short sentences, bullets, tables. No backstory, hedging or filler. Banned words are in [`docs/adr/README.md`](docs/adr/README.md).
- Never hard-wrap Markdown, commit messages or PR descriptions.
- Comments explain only the non-obvious why, carry no history (the commit records it), and fill to 120 columns.
- Commits: Conventional Commits, imperative subject, at most one or two sentences of why. Skip the body when the subject says it all.
